interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the chord's slope settling on 6 m per s as the chord swings towards the tangent, when you shrink the gap between its two points at 3 s.
interactive.title: A chord that becomes a tangent
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one graph, the speeding boat from the last lesson, f(x) = x² metres after x seconds, where x² means x × x. Point P sits on the curve at 3 s and 9 m and stays put. Point Q can be dragged along the curve, and the chord from P to Q is drawn with its Δx and Δy triangle and a readout of Δy ÷ Δx in m per s, the chord's slope. A slider shrinks the gap between the two points, Δx, through 1 s, 0.5 s, 0.1 s and 0.01 s, and a small table beside the graph fills in the chord's slope at each gap: 7, 6.5, 6.1 and 6.01 m per s. Each one comes from the rule. For a gap of 0.5 s, Q is at 3.5 s and 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25 m, so Δy = 12.25 − 9 = 3.25 m and 3.25 ÷ 0.5 = 6.5 m per s. As the gap shrinks the chord swings round towards one line through P, the tangent, drawn dashed with slope 6. Dragging Q to the left of P gives chords that end at 3 s, which read 5, 5.9 and 5.99 m per s, coming up to 6 from below. A zoom lens magnifies the curve around P, and each zoom makes the curve look straighter, until it is hard to tell from the tangent. Later screens use the draining tank from the last lesson, f(x) = 2(10 − x)² litres after x minutes, with its chord slopes shown in a table so no working with its rule is needed. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the graph.
interactive.ignores: The boat's and the tank's rules are example rules, chosen so the numbers come out exactly. The slider stops at a few gaps, so the chord gets close to the tangent and the settled value is read from the pattern in the table. A real speed or level record has small wobbles and a gap between readings, so its chords stop settling once the gap is shorter than the readings allow. Not every graph settles to one number: at a sharp corner, chords from the left and from the right settle on different numbers, and there is no single rate there.[^9]

explain.text:
The rate at an instant is what the average rate settles on as you shrink the stretch you average over. Take the speeding boat from the last lesson, f(x) = x² metres after x seconds. The chord from 3 s to 4 s gives 16 − 9 = 7 m per s. That is an average over a whole second, and the boat was speeding up all through that second, so 7 m per s is more than it was doing as the clock passed 3 s.

Keep P at 3 s and slide Q towards it. From 3 s to 3.5 s, f(3.5) = 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25 m, so Δy = 12.25 − 9 = 3.25 m over Δx = 0.5 s, which is 6.5 m per s. From 3 s to 3.1 s it is 0.61 ÷ 0.1 = 6.1 m per s, and from 3 s to 3.01 s it is 0.0601 ÷ 0.01 = 6.01 m per s. Each shorter chord averages over less of the speeding up, so its slope is a better estimate of the rate at 3 s itself.[^1] Look at the table: in every column the amount above 6 is the gap itself, 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01, so shrinking the gap shrinks the extra towards nothing, and the next lesson shows why. Chords that end at 3 s, from 2 s, 2.9 s and 2.99 s, read 5, 5.9 and 5.99 m per s, a little below 6 because the boat was slower before 3 s, and they come up towards 6 from below. You cannot simply make the gap zero, because then Δy and Δx are both 0, and 0 ÷ 0 has no answer. So the speed at 3 s is defined as the number these average speeds settle on as the gap shrinks, their [[limit]].[^2] Here it is 6 m per s exactly, not 'nearly 6': each chord from the right reads a little above 6, and you can bring it as close to 6 as you like by shrinking the gap. That settled number is the [[instantaneous rate of change]] at that point, which calculus calls the derivative there.[^3] Textbooks make 'settles on' exact with a formal definition of a limit, which this lesson leaves out.

As Q closes on P, the chord swings round towards one line through P with slope 6, the [[tangent]] at P: the tangent is the limit of the chords.[^4] Zoom in on P and y = x² looks straighter and straighter until it is hard to tell from the tangent, which is why the tangent's slope is the curve's rate there. Touching the curve once is not what makes the tangent. The upright line through P also meets y = x² just once, and it has no slope, because along it Δx is 0, so Δy ÷ Δx cannot be worked out. The rate is what the number means, and the tangent is a picture of it. One calculus teacher, writing for the Mathematical Association of America, argues that learners should not base their understanding of the derivative on the slope of the tangent.[^5]

A small change gets a small delta, δ, so a short chord's slope is written δy/δx. Its limiting value as δx shrinks towards zero is written dy/dx, read 'dee y by dee x'.[^6] The notation comes from the difference in y divided by the difference in x,[^7] and it is common in engineering and physics.[^8] At each point it is one symbol for one number, and its d's do not cancel to give y ÷ x: at 3 s, y ÷ x is 9 ÷ 3 = 3, but dy/dx = 6 m per s, in metres per second because y is in metres and x in seconds. **The rate at an instant is the number the slope of a chord settles on as its two points slide together, written dy/dx, the limiting value of δy/δx.[^6]**

analogy.text: A motor running up to speed is turning faster every moment. Count its shaft's turns over a whole minute and you get its average speed over that minute, which hides the running up. Count over shorter and shorter windows that start at the same moment and the averages settle on one number, the speed it was doing at that moment.
analogy.breaks: A turn count is a whole number, so over a very short window it reads 0 or 1 and the counting error swamps the answer: a real count gets worse, not better, once the window is too short. The maths has no smallest gap, which is how it gets the rate exactly.

practice.text:
- Pick the instant and work out y there.
- Take a chord forward from it with a small gap, and work out Δy ÷ Δx.
- Shrink the gap, say ten times, and work it out again. Do it once more.
- Do the same with chords that end at the instant, starting just before it.
- Read off the number both sides settle on, with its unit, the y unit per x unit. That is dy/dx there. If the two sides settle on different numbers, as at a sharp corner, there is no single rate at that point.[^9]

**Rules of thumb:** A rate at an instant is a settled average, so shrink the gap; do not set it to zero, because 0 ÷ 0 has no answer. Say what the number means in its units: how many metres per second, or litres per minute, at that moment.

**Worked example:** The draining tank from the last lesson holds f(x) = 2(10 − x)² litres after x minutes, so 128 L at 2 min. Forward chords with gaps of 0.1 and 0.01 min read −31.8 and −31.98 L per min. Chords ending at 2 min, from 1.9 and 1.99 min, read −32.2 and −32.02 L per min. Both sides settle on −32 L per min, so at 2 minutes the tank is losing 32 litres a minute, and the minus says it is emptying.

**From readings:** with real readings the gap cannot shrink below the time between readings, so the chord across the closest readings either side of the instant is an estimate, and you say so.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the height as the rate. 128 L is how much is in the tank, not how fast it is changing.
- Stopping at the last chord. −31.98 L per min is still an average over 0.01 min; the rate is −32.
- Setting the gap to zero. Then Δy and Δx are both 0, and 0 ÷ 0 tells you nothing.
- Cancelling the d's. dy/dx is not y ÷ x: 128 ÷ 2 = 64 is neither the size nor the sign of the rate.
- Calling the rate 'nearly' the settled number. The limit is exact: −32 L per min.
